extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers preparing novel submissions (e.g., Discoveries entrants) and general creative-writing students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on crafting the first sentence(s) of a novel to hook readers — focusing on introducing character, establishing time/place, setting tone/genre, and using sentence-level techniques. Includes many annotated examples from published novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce a protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: A really great opening sentence should introduce us to a protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meet the character early so readers know who the story will be about. Example: David Nicholls' You Are Here (‘…Marnie had never thought that she’d be lonely.’) is praised because we meet Marnie in the very first breath. The piece notes that naming (giving a surname, positioning the name first) signals importance — e.g. Still Life’s opening places Evelyn first and gives her a surname to mark her centrality. This strategy helps focus the reader on character-driven stories. Not every opener must do this, but it’s a clear, effective option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish time and place
rubrics_metrics.description: A great opening line can tell us when and where the story is happening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situating the reader immediately (time/place) helps orient them to the storyworld. The article lists this as one of the three core functions of the first line. Use concrete cues if setting is central to the story’s appeal, but be aware that withholding specific location can instead shift focus to character (see specificity vs vagueness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Set the tone and show the genre
rubrics_metrics.description: A really great opening sentence should set the tone for the novel and show us what genre we’re in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signal genre and tone early through diction and image. Example: Psalm for the Wild-Built uses 'robot consciousness' to indicate science fiction and a contemplative, humorous tone. Tone-setting can be subtle (voice, irony, rhythm) or explicit (referenced objects/terms). The post emphasises this as one of the core three goals of an opening line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entice the reader to keep reading (hook)
rubrics_metrics.description: Your opening line will help readers at every stage of your writing journey decide whether to read on or put your book down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The primary practical purpose of the first line is to compel continuation. That can be achieved via curiosity, surprise, voice, stakes, humour, or image. The post frames the opening line as the moment readers decide to continue — make it carry enough intrigue or promise to justify turning the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create immediate questions and stakes (in medias res)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with action or a startling image that immediately raises questions and stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Will of the Many (‘I am dangling… my father’s blood-slicked grip…’) throws readers straight into a life-or-death situation, provoking immediate questions (who, why, how) and heightened stakes, which compel reading. Use active situations or arresting physical detail to generate curiosity and urgency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a distinctive narrator voice/persona
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the first line to embed the reader in a character’s voice or an unusual narratorial stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voice can be humorous, wry, deadpan, philosophical, etc., and becomes a hook in itself. Examples: Evie Wyld’s ghostly narrator (‘I do not believe in ghosts… since my death…’) immediately establishes voice and premise; Remarkably Bright Creatures introduces Marcellus the octopus narrator to surprise and intrigue. A compelling voice often carries readers forward even when plot details are thin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a striking image or symbol that signals themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with an image or symbolic object that encapsulates or hints at broader themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Notes on an Execution (‘You are a fingerprint.’) uses a small, authoritative image that evokes crime, identity, and inherited trauma. A well-chosen image can operate on multiple levels (literal plot signifier and thematic resonance). Make the image suggestive rather than merely decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ sentence rhythm and punctuation purposefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentence length, rhythm, and punctuation can create mood and echo content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog highlights how dashes and rhythm can mirror meaning (Western Lane’s dashes resembling a squash serve) and how a long, rambling sentence can convey breathlessness or overwhelm (Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow’s extended opening). Deliberate syntactic choices (long vs short sentences, parenthetical asides, punctuation patterns) are tools to embody tone and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be unconventional or surprising when it serves the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment with unusual narrators, unexpected perspectives, or odd premises in your opening line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post celebrates bold, unapologetic openings: an octopus narrator, a ghost who doesn’t believe in ghosts, or a protagonist reinventing themselves. Unconventional openings can immediately mark a novel as distinctive. The authors stress that not all great openings are short and snappy — some break 'rules' to striking effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specificity and naming intentionally (who vs where)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to be specific about place or to withhold specifics to refocus attention onto character or theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Still Life’s opener is not precise about location in the Tuscan hills; by avoiding exactness the line shifts focus to 'who' and signals character-driven energy. Conversely, specific time/place cues can anchor a plot-driven opening. Choose the approach that best serves your novel’s emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use humour, surprise, and irony as hooks
rubrics_metrics.description: A witty or surprising first line can generate immediate engagement and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Evie Wyld’s opening elicited laughter and immediate grip; the article praises humour and surprise as quick ways to engage readers. Humour often works when it is anchored to voice or to an unexpected juxtaposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules are flexible — openings can combine strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: These are not hard and fast rules; some authors choose experimental approaches and some manage to do all three of the core tasks at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post explicitly states that openings may introduce character, place, and tone simultaneously or may subvert those expectations. Use the different strategies (voice, image, stakes, rhythm, specificity) in combination as appropriate. The multiple annotated examples demonstrate a range of successful approaches rather than prescribing a single formula.
